newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Second Indonesia riot trials start in Jakarta.
newsitem.headline: Second Indonesia riot trials start in Jakarta.

text.p: A second group of supporters of ousted Indonesian minority party leader Megawati Sukarnoputri appeared in court on Monday accused of assault and disobeying police orders as a result of July 27 violence in Jakarta.
Witnesses said Megawati, who was ousted as leader of the minority Indonesian Democratic Party (DPI), was at the court.
Megawati is the daughter of Indonesia's late founding president Sukarno.
A government-backed faction led by deputy parliamentary speaker Surjadi took over the party at a rebel congress in June.
Hundreds of riot police and troops guarded the Central Jakarta District Court on Monday, but there were no reports of violence.
Court clerk Budiman told Reuters the 60 people in court on Monday were being tried under the same charges and conditions as 64 accused who went on trial last Wednesday.
Lawyers said the charges relate to violence at the PDI headquarters, when Surjadi supporters backed by security forces moved in to evict Megawati adherents.

They said the charges did not relate to subsequent rioting in central Jakarta during which five people died and a number of buildings were burned in the worst violence in the city in more than two decades.
Chants of "We will win" from among 100 Megawati supporters echoed through the court.
A defence lawyer said that if the trials proceeded as normal, they could last about two months. But the defence had asked that they be speeded up.
Megawati said last week she had promised to attend the trials to demonstrate her belief that the accused were innocent.
The 124 accused are charged with using violence against people and property, and disobeying police orders to disperse on July 27 while occupying the PDI headquarters.

The official National Commission on Human Rights said in a report on Saturday on the July riots that the attack by 200 Surjadi supporters on the building with the cooperation of the security forces triggered the violence.
The human rights commission said five people died, 149 were injured and 23 remained missing as a result of the subsequent riots, which are still under investigation.

Defence laywers complained last week that none of the Surjadi group had been charged for initiating the attack on the PDI building. The commission also called on the government not to discriminate and to take action against the Surjadi supporters who attacked the headquarters.
The police have denied taking sides in the PDI dispute.
The military had said four people died in the riots and no one was missing. It said on Monday it would not comment on the commission report, but said if the figures differed "we will recheck" them.
The private Indonesian Legal Aid Foundation said the commission report could not be regarded as the final word as much information was still missing.
